title: Yudhishthira's dog
hookLine: the Mahabharata nears its end on a mountain road, with a dog walking behind a king
carry: dharma: never abandon one who trusts you
tomorrow: what did Yashoda see inside little Krishna's mouth?

lines: FIVE BROTHERS, DRAUPADI, AND A DOG.
cards: Near the end of the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and Draupadi leave their kingdom on foot. A dog falls in behind them and keeps walking. At last they turn north, toward the mountains.
On the slope, one walker falls, then another, then another. Yudhishthira, the eldest, keeps going and does not look back. Only the dog is still beside him when a chariot comes down to meet him.
This week's days share one name, the summit sit: each climbs back to one stretch of the year and sits there. Today, the great story.

teach.h: THE BOOK OF THE GREAT JOURNEY.
teach.b: The walk has a book of its own inside the epic, the Book of the Great Journey.
As each walker falls, Bhima asks his brother why, and Yudhishthira names a cause: a pride, a partiality, an appetite, something each one carried the whole way up. He does not stop to mourn.

teach.h: ONE BY ONE, THE WALKERS FALL.
teach.b: Then Indra, king of the gods, arrives in his chariot and invites Yudhishthira to rise to heaven in his own body. One condition: the dog stays behind. Yudhishthira refuses.

In the story's words, paraphrased: to abandon one who is devoted to you, one who is frightened and has no other refuge, is a grave wrong, and he will not do it, not even for heaven. Indra argues. Yudhishthira holds.
And then the dog changes form.
It was Dharma himself, the god of righteousness, who in the story is Yudhishthira's own father, testing his son again, as he once did as the Yaksha at the lake.
Now see the whole story from up here: the dice game, the forest years, the battlefield and the Gita spoken on it. A story that size could have closed on a war.
Near its end it stops instead on a tired man who will not leave a dog on a mountain.

teach.h: NEVER ABANDON ONE WHO TRUSTS YOU.
teach.b: That is a teaching the tradition holds high: you do not abandon one who has come to you for refuge, for any reward.
Whatever else dharma means across all those books, this test of it is small, and personal, and costs a great deal.

how: The Mahabharata lives in recitations, retellings, plays and television serials; the story of Yudhishthira refusing heaven without the dog is retold as a teaching about loyalty and dharma.

o: right conduct, tested in who you won't leave behind
the fate each person is born unable to change
a reward in heaven for a life of good deeds

games.q: the great journey — tap the pairs.
p: offers heaven, but not for the dog

s: in the story, Yudhishthira leaves the dog behind to enter heaven
he refuses heaven rather than abandon one who is devoted to him.
the dog turns out to be Dharma, Yudhishthira's father in the story
the dog changes form: it was Dharma himself, testing him.
Yudhishthira turns back to mourn each brother as he falls
he names a cause when Bhima asks, and walks on without looking back.

games.q: you are Yudhishthira. Indra's chariot is waiting to take you to heaven, but he says the dog cannot come. what do you do?
o: leave the dog and climb into the chariot.
refuse heaven rather than abandon the dog.
ask Indra for a day to think it over.
games.why: he refuses: abandoning one who is devoted and has no other refuge is a wrong he won't commit, even for heaven. Then the dog reveals itself as Dharma.

practice: Let the great story walk past you, one figure at a time: Bhishma, Kunti, Karna, Draupadi, Arjuna, Gandhari, Yudhishthira; if one stays, notice who it is, and let that be all right.
In the last breaths, bring to mind someone who has walked beside you through a hard stretch of your own road. Just their face.

wordCard.voice: Dharma. Right conduct, tested once more at the end of the great story, in a king who would not leave a dog on the mountain.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dharma, right order and right conduct; also the name of the god who takes the dog's form.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma: never abandon one who trusts you. Tomorrow, a smaller house, and a child's open mouth. Go gently.
